title: Client feedback by case phase: when to ask PI clients
summary: When should PI firms ask clients for feedback? Ask at fixed points in the case, read scores by phase and case manager, and follow up fast. See how Hona helps.
body_markdown:
Most firms ask clients for feedback once, at the end. The settlement check has cleared, the client is relieved, the score comes back high, and the review link goes out. The firm learns almost nothing about the year before.


When should a personal injury firm ask clients for feedback? Ask a short question at a few fixed points during the case, read the answers by phase and by case manager, and call every client who gives a low score.


## Why the end-of-case survey tells you so little


After the payout, a satisfaction score mostly measures the payout. The problems that shape a client's experience happened months earlier: a text that sat unanswered during treatment, a long silence while the demand was out. By the time the case closes, none of it can be fixed.


The client who was frustrated in month four usually just wanted to know what was happening. Nobody asked.


## Where to ask during the case


Pick the moments when frustration tends to build, and ask the same thing every time. One rating question and one open question are enough.


- **After sign-up.** Does the client understand what happens next and who to contact?
- **During treatment.** This is the longest stretch of most cases, and the easiest place for a client to feel forgotten.
- **While the demand is out.** Clients hear little while your firm waits on records and the insurer, so a check here catches frustration early.
- **During long negotiations.** This is where repeat "where's my case?" calls start.


## Read the answers by phase and by person


A firm-wide average hides the problem. Break the results down by phase, case manager, office, and language.


- **Low scores in one phase.** Point to a process gap, such as no updates during a stretch where nothing visible happens.
- **Low scores under one case manager.** Usually mean too many cases, not a bad employee.
- **The same comment again and again.** "Nobody calls me back" tells you the fix in the client's own words.


Then close the loop. Give one person the job of calling every low score within two business days. Label the comment box clearly as private feedback, too. Some clients assume it is a public review.
